title: The Small Glasshouse
premise: Paloma Almeida, a Portuguese-to-English translator in a fading coastal town, discovers behind her late grandmother's wardrobe a bundle of letters never delivered — correspondence between her grandmother and a man who vanished during the dictatorship years. As Paloma translates them, she realizes the final letter contains a sentence her grandmother deliberately left untranslated, one that names the man who betrayed the family and implicates Paloma's own father in his disappearance. Translating it means choosing between the family she has left and the truth that could dissolve what remains of her identity; when she finally renders the sentence into English, she mails copies to every living relative, ending the silence at the cost of her brother's love, and begins writing her own letters — this time addressed, signed, and sent.
about_author: Mara Voss is the pen name of a former court interpreter who spent a decade translating testimony in immigration hearings before turning to fiction. She writes about language as both shelter and betrayal from a house within earshot of the Atlantic.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. We meet her at a funeral reception where she deploys her perfected smile to deflect condolences, revealing her habit of retreat and her fraying relationship with Portuguese, which slips from her mid-sentence. Her brother Tomás urges her to clear out their grandmother's house before developers take it. Beat: loneliness disguised as composure.

chapters.title: What the Wardrobe Kept
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Clearing the bedroom alone, she finds a false back panel in the wardrobe and a tin box: forty-one letters, unsent, bundled with string, all addressed to a name she doesn't recognize — Duarte Fonseca. The last envelope is sealed but stamped 'não enviar.' Beat: the thrill and dread of an opened door.

chapters.title: A Translator's Ethics
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, with flashbacks to her training. She tells herself reading dead people's mail is harmless scholarship, but hesitates over the first letter anyway. A client call interrupts — a legal translation due Friday — establishing the professional life she uses as armor. She reads letter one. Beat: curiosity outrunning conscience.

chapters.title: Duarte
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The early letters (1971) reveal a warm, clandestine romance between her young grandmother Inês and Duarte, a printer who publishes forbidden pamphlets. Paloma recognizes the handwriting's confidence, nothing like her grandmother's careful later script. She visits the town archive; Duarte Fonseca has no death record. Beat: the past becoming a person.

chapters.title: Tomás Wants to Sell
chapters.summary: Tomás's POV. He arrives with a realtor's folder and finds the house in disarray, papers everywhere. He accuses Paloma of sabotaging the sale out of sentimentality. Their argument exposes old wounds: he stayed near their father, she fled abroad for years. He notices the box; she lies badly. Beat: sibling fracture widening.

chapters.title: The Letters Turn
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The 1972 letters darken — coded language, missed meetings, Inês pregnant and terrified. Then a gap of eight months. When the letters resume, Inês writes to a changed address, and the tone is grief without explanation. Paloma cross-references dates with a history of the local arrests. Beat: dread accumulating like weather.

chapters.title: The Father Who Paid
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, digging through municipal records and an old neighbor's memory. She learns her grandfather — her father's father — was a regime informant, and that Duarte was arrested weeks after Inês's last meeting with him. The implication lands sideways: her family's comfort was purchased with someone's disappearance. Beat: inheritance revealed as debt.

chapters.title: The Untranslatable Sentence
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The final letter, dated 1974, contains one sentence Inês never translated even for herself, written in a private shorthand they invented together. Paloma can decode most of it; three words resist her. She works through the night, and by dawn understands its shape if not its full meaning: it names what her grandfather did, and asks forgiveness of no one. Beat: vertigo at the edge of knowing.

chapters.title: Client Work
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Forced back to her paid translation — a deportation affidavit for a young Angolan woman — she finds herself unable to render the woman's testimony flatly, inserting weight the source doesn't carry. Her supervisor flags it. The parallel becomes explicit: translation is never neutral; someone always decides what survives. Beat: craft and conscience colliding.

chapters.title: The Archive Clerk
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, with the clerk Rui as secondary presence. Rui, a retired teacher volunteering at the archive, remembers Duarte's printing shop and produces a photograph: Duarte alive in 1976, released, emigrated to Brazil. He didn't die; he was erased. Paloma feels the first real hope — and the first real obligation. Beat: a door opening outward.

chapters.title: Tomás Reads One Letter
chapters.summary: Tomás's POV. He returns unannounced, finds the letters, and reads one before Paloma can stop him. His reaction is not hers: he wants them burned, wants the sale finished, wants their father's memory protected. 'You weren't here,' he says. 'You don't know what it cost us to be quiet.' Beat: two legitimate griefs in collision.

chapters.title: The Glasshouse
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Title chapter. She recalls her grandmother's small glasshouse where cuttings were coaxed into root — visible growth, invisible roots. There she finds, taped under a bench, a note in Inês's hand: instructions never to send the letters, 'so that someone after me may choose.' The choice was always meant to be inherited. Beat: burden reframed as bequest.

chapters.title: Rio, Answered
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Through Rui and a genealogy society, she traces Duarte's daughter in Rio de Janeiro and writes — her first sent letter in the book. Weeks pass. The reply comes: Duarte died in 1998, but his daughter encloses something he kept fifty years — Inês's only delivered letter, and a question he asked on his deathbed: did she ever forgive herself? Beat: grief answered across decades.

chapters.title: What the Father Knew
chapters.summary: Tomás's POV. Confronted with the Rio evidence, Tomás finally admits what he learned caring for their dying father: the old man confessed once, drunk, to a phone call made in 1973. Tomás has carried it silently for six years. His anger at Paloma curdles into shame. Beat: the second generation's complicity exposed.

chapters.title: Deciding What Survives
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She attempts a full English translation of the final letter and fails repeatedly — each version either betrays Inês or flatters the family. She drafts, deletes, drafts again, mirroring her own life's evasions. Her supervisor's earlier rebuke returns: accuracy is a moral act. Beat: the translator's crucible.

chapters.title: The Sealed Envelope
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She steams open the envelope marked 'não enviar' expecting the decoded sentence; instead it holds a photograph of Duarte and a single line in Inês's plain hand: 'Tell them I chose him over my own safety, and lost him over my own fear.' The sentence Paloma feared was condemnation of her grandfather is also Inês's confession of abandonment. Beat: the revelation complicated, deepened.

chapters.title: Deadline
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converging. The developer's demolition notice arrives — thirty days. Tomás signs preliminary papers. Paloma must decide whether to translate publicly or let the house — and the letters' context — vanish quietly. The Angolan client's affidavit, meanwhile, is approved because of Paloma's 'unfaithful' fidelity. Beat: time forcing the ethical hand.

chapters.title: The Reading
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. At a small gathering in the glasshouse — Tomás, Rui, the client Amara, a handful of neighbors — Paloma reads the final letter aloud in Portuguese, then gives her English translation, including the untranslatable sentence rendered as faithfully as she can bear. Silence, then Tomás stands and adds what their father confessed. Beat: climax; speech breaking the inherited silence.

chapters.title: Aftermath, First Days
chapters.summary: Alternating Paloma and Tomás POVs. The fallout is quiet and real: an aunt stops calling, a cousin sends one furious message, but Amara asks Paloma to help with her asylum appeal, and Rui proposes archiving the letters properly. Tomás withdraws from the sale — then reconsiders, torn. Beat: cost itemized, meaning uncertain.

chapters.title: What Tomás Keeps
chapters.summary: Tomás's POV. Alone in the house, he rereads his grandmother's letters and finds in one a passage about him as a baby — tenderness he never suspected was recorded anywhere. He calls Paloma and, without apology or preamble, asks her to teach him the shorthand so he can read the rest himself. Beat: reconciliation without absolution.

chapters.title: The Last Translation
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She completes the definitive translation of all forty-one letters, adding translator's notes that admit every uncertainty — including the three words she never fully resolved. She donates the originals to the archive and keeps only photocopies. Writing to Duarte's daughter, she answers the deathbed question honestly: no, Inês never forgave herself; but she left the truth where someone might find it. Beat: acceptance of imperfect fidelity.

chapters.title: Letters, Addressed
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, closing frame echoing chapter one. At another reception, someone offers condolences and she lets the conversation run long instead of smiling it shut. In the rebuilt glasshouse of her rented flat, seedlings root visibly. She writes a letter to her estranged aunt — addressed, signed, stamped — and mails it. Some sentences, she now knows, are only survivable once spoken. Beat: resolution; language reclaimed as connection.
